practice.title: Overcoming Self-Cherishing
agreedSteps: Offer our body — overcome self-cherishing by offering our body to the Buddhas through helping Dharma flourish, with the specific intention of breaking down the self-cherishing mind. It's not just doing things for the Dharma center; it's doing them with the mind of offering our body as a servant to all the Buddhas.

Make a neglect list. Think: who has my self-cherishing made me neglect? Run through the list occasionally — not out of guilt, but to fuel a genuine wish to exorcise self-cherishing. Self-cherishing made me let this person down. Self-cherishing made me not be there for them. This builds a powerful, grounded motivation.

Identify a personal problem you're fed up with, link it to self-cherishing, and then sit with the wish to overcome self-cherishing. Don't run to the antidote — the wish itself is the object of meditation. When the wish is powerful enough, any Dharma tool you grab will land like a ton of bricks.
steps: Practice remembering that I and this body are not the same. I is just a name put on the body. The body is not the self. Read the View of the Transitory Collection section in How to Understand the Mind — it's a unique little emptiness teaching worth sitting with slowly, two lines at a time.

When making offerings, try doing it more rather than less. If visualization feels flat or disconnected, get indulgent with it — make it alive, make it 3D. Something clicks when you give yourself space to find the delight in it.
If you notice your delusions have a pattern — especially a nighttime pattern — try rotating your rhythm and routine. Delusions are dumb and feed on habits; break the pattern and they get confused.
practice.quote: If the wish is really, really powerful, any Dharma tool you grab will land like a ton of bricks.

commentary.title: Self-Cherishing Is Dangerous
content: This practice of offering our body is incredible, and it's everything. Because this practice is about overcoming self-cherishing, which is everything. We need to have a fear of continuing to identify and cherish this body as ourself. Not a fear of sickness, not a fear of death, not a fear of pain. A fear of cherishing this body as ourself. Which basically means feeling it's dangerous to keep thinking of this body as myself.

When we encounter a lot of sickness and pain, we know in that moment: if only I didn't think of this body as myself. If I saw it as my car, I wouldn't be having these kinds of problems. Your car can have serious issues, be dented and broken, whatever — but you don't hurt in the same way. Because we don't think, I am my car. But when we think, I am my body, we cherish our body as ourself. It's unbearable when it's in pain.

What if we get nerve pain that sets in today and never leaves until we die? That could happen very easily. There's just one day that it happens. It's not like you get a warning. As long as we think of this as ourself, we're in big trouble. This body is a pain magnet. The machinery breaks down. Having the mind of self-cherishing is more dangerous than any scary enemy, more dangerous than war. Then on the basis of that, we develop the thought: I want to exorcise this demon of self-cherishing from my mind.

commentary.title: The Wish Is the Object of Meditation
content: When we approach meditation, it's very nice to think problem–solution as a couplet. What are my lived problems that I'm just done with, that I despise, that I'm fed up with? Then all we have to do is link it to the solution. With self-cherishing it's particularly easy because every single problem on earth comes from self-cherishing.

The key is that the wish is the actual object of meditation. Many people go straight to, well, then how do I overcome it? They jump to some meditation on love, compassion, exchanging self with others. That's the next step. But if you don't stop at the wish and make it seared into the mind, what happens is you have a half-hearted interest, and you rush to a solution you're trying to do with a half-hearted interest, and it doesn't land. If the wish is really, really powerful, any Dharma tool you grab will land like a ton of bricks.

When we try a Dharma practice and it doesn't work, it's simply because we don't really want to do it. We're going through the motions. Basically, it's a lack of wishing faith. If we really, really want something, we remember it. It's not hard to remember something we really, really want. If you have an amazing date with the person of your dreams at 9 p.m. tonight, are you going to forget? There's no way. So if we don't remember Dharma, it's mostly just because we don't want to actually remember it. We just need a stronger wish.
commentary.quote: If we really, really want something, we just remember it. It's not hard to remember something we really, really want.

commentary.title: I Is Not the Body — Just a Name
content: It's very hard to oppose self-cherishing if we think the body and the I are one. One of the easiest things to do is start seeing that I and the body are not the same. I is just a name put on the body. The body is not the self. Geshe-la says we normally refer to our body and mind as 'my body' and 'my mind,' in a similar way to which we refer to our other possessions. This indicates that they are different from our I. The body and mind are the basis upon which we establish our I, not the I itself.

There's a passage in How to Understand the Mind about a child who is named Buddha by his parents. The child would grow up thinking, I am Buddha. But when he discovered that Buddha was someone free from the two obstructions, he would realize he was not an actual Buddha, but just an ordinary person with the name Buddha. Our situation is similar — we've always thought of ourselves as I and assumed that corresponding to this name, there was a real I. We search for this I and will not find it. Behind this I, there is nothing at all.

When the car accident happened today, a man came running up. He said, last week another car flipped here, and I was parked over here, and I was afraid, so I came to check on my car — and her name is Jenny. He just loved Jenny. And it was just a great teaching. There's no Jenny, right? But the second you put that name, it starts to feel like there's something there. It's just a name, just a word. And Buddha is saying, that's the same with I. It's no different than Jenny on the SUV.

commentary.title: We Are Not Our Delusions
content: If we get it totally clear that we are not the delusions, we won't have the problem of guilt about not having already overcome them. This isn't a throwaway point — it's a very profound thing that has to do with overcoming our self-grasping ignorance. Delusions are characteristics of a person's mind, not of the person. Since we can never find faults in sentient beings themselves, we can say that in this respect, sentient beings are like Buddhas.

All faults are coming from the delusions, not the I. I is just a label that has landed on a body and mind. So when we become guilty, we're still thinking the I is those delusions. We're still associating with the basis of imputation as the self. Getting a visceral sense of the separation between self and delusions is basically the same as meditating on the emptiness of the self. When we meditate on emptiness, we think: I am not my mind, I am not my body. Distinguishing between the delusions and the self is doing that part of the meditation. Once we stop imputing our I on the delusions, it becomes a billion times easier to work on them.

commentary.title: The Neglect List
content: The word 'neglecting' in the definition of self-cherishing is really important. Self-cherishing is thinking I am important while neglecting others. It's very useful to think: who has my self-cherishing made me neglect? Not out of guilt — but to fuel a genuine wish to exorcise self-cherishing. Self-cherishing made me let this person down. Self-cherishing made me not be there for them. Self-cherishing made me turn my back on that person. It's very grounding. It gets the mind out of the sky and back into reality.

There's an important distinction here: thinking about the harm done via delusions is useful when it comes from a virtue, not when it comes from self-lacerating guilt. Don't throw out the virtuous version of the activity along with the deluded version. It's the same as how caring what people think is harmful from attachment but essential from consideration for others. Or how saying something strong to someone is harmful from anger but necessary from a virtue. The same activity, two different minds. We don't want to throw out the version that comes from a virtue.

commentary.title: Sublime Offerings and Offering Our Practice
content: Sublime offerings are purer than ordinary visualized offerings — they're offerings actually manifested by superior beings. In One Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa, Milarepa wanted to test the Indian Pandit Padampa Sangye's spiritual powers, so he flew miraculously to a mountain and transformed himself into a flower near the roadside. When Padampa Sangye walked past, Milarepa thought the Indian had no powers of clairvoyance. But shortly after, the Pandit paused, turned around, walked back to the flower, kicked it sharply, and shouted, "You, Milarepa, stand up!" Milarepa immediately resumed his human form and greeted him warmly.

There is another sublime offering we can make right at this present moment: to practice the teachings we have received from our spiritual guide. Practicing Dharma is the one thing the Buddhas can't do for us. Our mental continuum is causally related — our guru can't hop into our continuum, because it's related to all of its previous moments. As the famous quote says, Buddha can't take our suffering from us like a thorn from a foot. So when we practice, it is the best offering. The Buddhas are so happy for us. They've been trying to get us to do this for billions of eons, and we've stubbornly refused. So when we're finally practicing — what a delight. Just crying of joy watching us practice. Just trying, just showing up. Amazing.

commentary.title: Dharma First — The Warrior's Plan
content: Shantideva throughout this text uses the image of a warrior in battle — putting on the armor and rushing into battle. When we step into any new adventure, the practice is to have a Dharma plan and charge in. Not charge in and then be a fair-weather Dharma fan calling for help after it all fell apart. Dharma first. Put on the helmet, get the shield, the sword, the chain mail, and charge into battle with Dharma.

When we do this, one of the key things is putting meditation practice first — not trying to fit it around everything else. When we put practice first, it reminds us that the other stuff just doesn't matter that much. And actually acting in that way reminds us that that's the truth of the situation.

commentary.title: Nighttime Delusions and Breaking the Pattern
content: Tired nighttime space is somewhere tip-top on the leaderboard for delusion breeding ground. There's often a tension debt that builds throughout the day, and at some point there's a critical mass where we snap and follow the delusion. Sometimes we feel like, I owe myself a little delusion time. I've been so virtuous today, I need to create the causes of suffering now.

Three things to try: one, don't accrue the tension debt throughout the day — just practice Dharma. Two, go to bed when we're tired. Don't distract to relax, because distraction is not relaxing — it's agitating. Three, rotate the rhythm and routine. Delusions feed on certain rhythms and routines, and if you break them, they don't trigger the same way. Delusions are very dumb — they're just ignorant minds. They're often not even smart enough to rejig if we mess up their normal playing field. Bring in a nighttime walk with no device. Sit at the dinner table instead of the couch. Save cleaning and organizing for the evening. The point is about changing the habits, the patterns.
